paras: The threatened lynching of John Jordan occurred at Frankfort, Kentucky, in August 1890, when Jordan, a Black man held in jail there on a charge of assaulting a little girl, was threatened with lynching. Officials placed an extra guard at the jail, and no attack on Jordan was reported. The episode is known only from a short wire item reprinted in out-of-state news digests.

Jordan, described in the reports as "a negro," was arrested on a charge of assaulting a little girl near Peak's Mill, Kentucky, an offense the Indianapolis Journal's version dated to "Tuesday." A fuller version of the same item, printed in Mississippi, described the charge as "the outrage of a little white girl."

While in jail at Frankfort, Jordan was reported to have confessed to the crime on August 7. The dispatch added that "there are threats of lynching, and an extra guard has been placed," without saying who made the threats or how many people were involved.
The coverage does not report what became of Jordan, whether he was tried, or whether the threats led to any further action.

The Indianapolis Journal printed the item on August 9 in its "Telegraphic Brevities" column, between a Chicago kerosene accident and Texas railroad washouts. Five days later the Brookhaven Leader in Mississippi ran nearly the same words among its "Condensed Telegrams," adding the date of the confession and the girl's race. Neither paper gave the item a headline or commented on it, and both stated Jordan's confession as fact, citing no source for it.
No Kentucky report and no Black-press coverage of the episode were found; what is known rests on this single dispatch.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of John Jordan
bases: The only reports describe 'threats of lynching' against a Black prisoner accused of assaulting a girl and an extra guard placed at the jail; no attack is reported (A1, A2).

No one was killed: the reports mention only 'threats of lynching' against Jordan, who was in jail under an extra guard (A1, A2). Who made the threats, how many, and whether anyone acted on them is not reported.
Both reports are versions of the same telegraphic brief, nearly word for word, printed in news-digest columns in Indiana and Mississippi (A1, A2); no independent or local account was found.
